claims.text: The transient ductile-brittle-ductile transition is driven by temperature-dependent LCO evolution in B2 and consequent changes in dislocation mobility at FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Intermediate-temperature aging orders or coarsens LCOs within B2.
Ordering or coarsening of B2 LCOs increases their anti-phase-boundary energy.
High APB energy in ordered domains creates a large barrier to dislocation shearing.
Ordered precipitates with high APB energy can strengthen an FCC-based HEA.
When B2 ordered domains cannot be sheared, dislocations bow around them by Orowan looping or pile up at FCC/B2 phase boundaries.
Dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries generate stress concentrations that exceed interface cohesive strength.
The pile-up-induced stress concentration nucleates cracks at interfaces or within B2 and causes macroscopic brittleness.
Increasing the aging temperature further dissociates LCOs, produces a less ordered state, or dissolves or transforms B2.
Higher temperature reduces the APB barrier or thermally enables domain shearing, thereby restoring ductility.
Annealing temperature and composition can control the length scale of ordered B2 plus disordered BCC decomposition and affect hardness.
Aging from 400°C to 700°C for 10 to 100 hours is an appropriate intermediate-ordering regime for typical FCC/B2 HEAs.
Ductility will exhibit an intermediate-temperature minimum, exemplified by a proposed peak-brittleness condition near 550°C.
Below the embrittlement regime, LCOs are insufficiently developed, whereas above it they dissolve or transform.
Fracture at peak brittleness will occur at FCC/B2 interfaces rather than at grain boundaries.
The embrittlement regime is bounded below by the onset of LCO formation and above by LCO dissolution or phase transformation.
A correlation between ductility loss and grain-boundary segregation, rather than bulk-B2 LCO evolution, would falsify the proposed LCO mechanism.
Ductility loss without an accompanying increase in phase-boundary dislocation pile-ups would falsify the proposed mechanism.
APT can map the relevant LCO density and distinguish bulk-B2 ordering from grain-boundary segregation.
APB energy can be estimated from diffraction or TEM measurements in the proposed experiment.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis allows crack nucleation within the B2 phase, but the prediction specifies FCC/B2 interfacial cracking, while the falsification rule says transgranular cleavage within B2 would make the mechanism incorrect.

Mechanical testing may occur at room temperature after aging, yet recovery is partly attributed to thermal activation overcoming the APB barrier at the higher aging temperature. That transient thermal activation would not necessarily persist during a subsequent room-temperature test unless a retained structural change is demonstrated.
